_comment: LOCAL TRUST POLICY for tee-claude. YOU install and approve this file.
Copy it to ~/.tee-claude/policy.json and edit it.
It is never fetched from the endpoint being verified. The endpoint may
PROPOSE a change to the served model, and tee-claude will show you a diff
and ask you to type yes before recording it here (keeping a .bak). It can
never change endpoint_host, the TLS pins or the issuer expectation: those
are what make 'this is the right endpoint' mean anything, and they only
ever change because you changed them.
_comment_endpoint: The HOSTNAME is pinned here and is never discovered. Only the TCP PORT is
looked up at launch, from the DNS TXT record below, because the machine's
public IP and port both change every time it restarts (which is nightly).
Consequence worth understanding: anyone who tampers with that TXT record
can move you to a different PORT on a host that still has to pass every
certificate check below. They cannot move you to a different host.
_comment_model: The model you have approved, and the limits the launcher configures Claude
Code with. 491520 input / 32768 output is the real split on this deployment:
the model's 524288-token window minus the 32768-token output reservation.
_comment_tls: tls_spki_sha256 pins the endpoint's public key, and it is FILLED IN below.
Where that value came from, and why that matters: it was shipped to you inside
this repository — release tarball, checksum-verified against the release's
SHA256SUMS before install.sh unpacked it. That is a DIFFERENT root of trust from
the certificate api.mynacloud.com presents. So when the launcher compares the two
at check [10], two independent sources have to agree.
What it is NOT: trust-on-first-use. TOFU would be pinning whatever the endpoint
happens to present the first time you connect, with nothing to compare it to.
Nothing here does that, and there is no flag that will.
You can verify it yourself, and you are encouraged to:
tee-claude --print-spki
prints what the endpoint is presenting right now. It should equal the value below.
IF IT DOES NOT MATCH, DO NOT EDIT THIS FILE TO MAKE THE ERROR GO AWAY. A mismatch
is one of exactly two things: a key rotation you were not told about, or someone
presenting a certificate that is not ours. Both are worth an email before a paste.
Ask the operator which one it is. Overwriting the pin with whatever the endpoint
showed you converts a caught problem into an uncaught one.
Emptying this field, or setting it back to REPLACE-ME, makes check [10] FAIL and
the launcher refuse to start. That is deliberate: an unpinned key means the only
thing between you and any CA-issued certificate for this name is the public CA
system, and a launcher whose product is verification should not treat that as
fine.
expected_issuer_* asserts the certificate is OURS and not merely valid. This
host's DNS is on Cloudflare in DNS-only mode. If that record is ever switched to
proxied, Cloudflare terminates TLS and presents its own certificate: the chain
would still verify and the hostname would still match, while a third party read
every prompt in plaintext. Check [11] is what makes that loud instead of
invisible. It is pinned to the exact intermediate that issued the current
certificate rather than a general Let's Encrypt shape.
_future_tee_pins: Once the endpoint runs in a Confidential VM these become enforceable and
checks [14]-[34] stop reporting UNSUPPORTED. They are intentionally absent
now rather than present-and-ignored, so the policy never implies a
guarantee the verifier cannot actually establish.
